subject: Cooking
title: The Five-Second Rule Is Fiction
description: A quick, practical guide to The Five-Second Rule Is Fiction.

hook.text: Drop food on the floor? Quick — five-second rule! Except bacteria don't have a stopwatch.

buildup.text: The myth assumes bacteria need time to transfer to food. The reality is less comforting.

discovery.text: Rutgers University found bacteria transfer to food in less than one second — moisture and surface type matter more.

twist.text: Wet foods on tile pick up far more bacteria than dry foods on carpet — time is the least important factor.

climax.text: A 2016 study tested 128 scenarios — in every single case, some bacterial transfer occurred instantly.

punchline.text: The five-second rule is zero seconds wrong.

quiz.question: How quickly do bacteria transfer to dropped food?

details.summary: Bacteria transfer to dropped food in milliseconds, not five seconds. Research shows contamination begins instantly on contact. Wet foods pick up more bacteria than dry foods, and smooth surfaces transfer more than rough ones. The five-second rule provides zero actual safety margin.
details.whyItMatters: While the actual risk from briefly dropped food is usually low in clean homes, the five-second rule creates a false sense of timed safety that does not exist. The real factors are surface cleanliness and food moisture.
takeaways: Bacteria transfer in under one second of surface contact
Wet foods pick up significantly more bacteria than dry foods
Floor cleanliness matters far more than pickup speed

faq.question: How quickly do bacteria actually transfer to food?
faq.answer: Rutgers University researchers found bacteria transfer begins in less than one second. Longer contact does increase the total number transferred, but even instant contact moves thousands of bacteria. The speed of pickup provides no meaningful protection whatsoever.

faq.question: Is eating dropped food actually dangerous?
faq.answer: In a reasonably clean home, brief floor contact rarely causes illness. The immune system handles small bacterial exposures daily. The real risk depends on what is on the floor. Hospital floors, public restrooms, and kitchen floors near raw meat pose genuine contamination risks.
